title: Activated Long-Term Memory
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane, a math teacher, uses the idea of activated long-term memory to explain how to get repetition right for math facts and reading fluency. He starts from the simple model of the mind, in which a fact moves through working memory and is strengthened by retrieval from long-term memory. Retrieval is far more efficient than simple repetition, but struggling students often fall back on skip-counting, which consumes working memory and builds little. Practicing a narrow set of facts, such as just the fives, brings the same fact back within minutes, so it is still activated and retrieval is likelier to succeed. He draws a parallel with repeated reading and orthographic mapping, noting that the research is contested and that repetition only works when paired with teacher modeling and targeted instruction. He closes by defending these unglamorous routines as efficient, crucial for some students, and compatible with teaching meaning and joy.
points: Retrieval, not repetition alone, secures learning, but retrieval only helps when it succeeds, so students who cannot recall a fact gain little from a mixed worksheet.
Activated long-term memory is the window of seconds to minutes when a fact has left working memory but is still easy to retrieve, and short, focused practice exploits it.
Narrow practice such as only the fives gives several repetitions per fact in a few minutes, replacing the once-every-two-weeks exposure of a fully mixed sheet.
Repeated reading works only when paired with anticipating tricky words, teacher modeling, and listening in to adjust the next round.
These routines are helpful for all, harmful for none, and crucial for some, and they do not displace meaning, connection, or joy in reading.
quotes: Much more efficient is to make use of that “remembering” arrow in the diagram above, getting students to retrieve the fact from long-term memory.
If they’re successful, they strengthen long-term memory. If they fall back on skip-counting, they don’t.
It’s not in working memory, but because the student was recently thinking about it the fact is much easier to retrieve from long-term memory.
The parallel here is that we absolutely want students to be sounding out words that they don’t know. We just don’t want them sounding out words forever.

Dig in and the message is: simply asking students to read a passage multiple times is not enough. Instead, that repeated reading needs to be paired with teacher modeling and targeted instruction to help students read words successfully.
This is the heart of teaching: I’m not just giving students a task, I’m monitoring and responding in the moment to emphasize what I want students to learn.

The reality is, students have a hard time understanding the meaning of fractions if they can’t remember what 3 x 5 is. Students have a hard time learning to love reading if they need to effortfully decode every word on the page.
